analysis.one_liner: Cuts the federal estate tax rate nearly in half, from 40% to 20%.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: it was referred to House committees in April 2024 and got no vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would lower the top federal tax rate on large inherited estates, large gifts, and generation-skipping transfers from 40% to 20%, cutting the tax nearly in half. It also exempts the revenue loss from automatic budget rules that normally require new tax cuts to be paid for. It would apply retroactively to deaths and gifts after the end of 2022. The bill was introduced in April 2024 and referred to the Ways and Means and Budget Committees, where it stayed until the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The main gainers are heirs to the largest estates — families whose inheritances are big enough to be subject to the federal estate tax — and wealthy people making very large taxable gifts. Because the rate applies to the biggest transfers, the value of the cut rises with the size of the estate; a family passing on tens of millions of dollars would save millions in tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a single 20% rate for the tax on estates, gifts, and generation-skipping transfers, replacing the current top rate of 40% [S2].
The change applies retroactively, to estates of people dying, generation-skipping transfers, and gifts made after December 31, 2022 [S3].

The bill exempts its budgetary effects from the Pay-As-You-Go scorecards, so the revenue loss would not automatically trigger spending offsets under either the statutory PAYGO law or the FY2018 budget resolution [S2] [S3].

Only the largest estates and gifts are subject to the federal estate and gift tax at all, so the rate cut reaches only the wealthiest households' transfers; smaller inheritances are already exempt under current-law exclusion amounts.

analysis.who_pays: If enacted, the federal government would collect less revenue from the largest estates and gifts. Reduced revenue must ultimately be made up by other taxpayers, by borrowing, or by lower federal spending, so the cost would be spread across everyone who relies on or pays federal taxes.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the top rate from 40% to 20% would substantially reduce federal revenue from the largest estates and gifts, and the bill explicitly waives the budget rules that would otherwise force the cut to be paid for [S2] [S3].

The retroactive effective date (to transfers after December 31, 2022) would deliver refunds or reduced liability for transfers already made or Estates already settled under the 40% rate, adding to the cost [S3].

Because the federal estate tax applies only above the current exclusion amount, the tax cut would flow exclusively to a small number of very large estates and large gift-givers, not to the vast majority of families.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concentrated: a large, permanent tax reduction for heirs to the biggest estates, made retroactive and shielded from PAYGO. The cost is a broad revenue loss borne by everyone else through future taxes, borrowing, or spending choices. For ordinary households, who are already exempt from the estate tax, the bill offers essentially nothing; for the wealthiest families it offers millions in savings per estate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means and Budget Committees, and neither committee ever acted on it before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-TX) introduced the Estate Tax Rate Reduction Act on April 15, 2024 [S1] [S5].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the House Budget Committee [S5].
The bill drew a single cosponsor, one House Democrat [S4].
No further action was taken — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never became law, current-law estate taxation at the 40% top rate remains in place, so the general taxpayer is better off than under the bill, while heirs to very large estates did not get the tax cut they would have received. The bill's backers lost nothing but the proposal itself.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal taxpayers; estate-tax cut never enacted

for.name: Rep. Jodey C. Arrington
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member (Budget Committee chairman)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cut the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer tax rate from 40% to 20% and shield the revenue loss from PAYGO rules.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; only one House Democrat signed on.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was Republican-sponsored with a single Democratic cosponsor and no recorded opposition votes, because it never advanced far enough to get one.

industries.industry: Heirs to the largest estates and wealthy families making large gifts
industries.note: The 20% rate would cut their tax on large inheritances and gifts nearly in half, retroactively, with the revenue loss shifted to the general budget. Ordinary families are already below the estate-tax threshold and get nothing.

industries.industry: Estate-planning attorneys, wealth managers, and trusts-and-estates professionals
industries.note: A lower transfer-tax rate would reduce the value of elaborate avoidance planning, but lower rates can also spur more lifetime gifting and trust activity among the wealthy. The bill never advanced, so any effect is hypothetical.
